title: Influence of a 100-mile ultramarathon on heart rate and heart rate variability
authors: Paech C, Schrieber S, Daehnert I, Schmidt-Hellinger PJ, Wolfarth B, Wuestenfeld J, Thouet T
population: 28 runners (25 men, 3 women) in a 100-mile ultramarathon, 24 h Holter ECG one week before, immediately after and after a week of recovery
findings: A rise in baseline heart rate (18.98%) immediately after the run.
A significant drop in the SD of all normal RR intervals (7.12%) 1 week after the run.
Full return of HRV to the athletes' baseline did not occur within 1 week.

Authors conclude HRV might be a suitable parameter to evaluate the state of recovery after a 100-mile run but does not help to quantify it, since damage to the tendomuscular system primarily characterises recovery. No significant differences between finishers and non-finishers in the analysed parameters.
limitations: Small sample, 3 women; only one follow-up point (1 week), so the time to HRV normalisation is unknown; 24 h Holter HRV is not the same as a morning wearable reading; abstract gives no per-metric values beyond the percentages.
implications: One week after a 100-mile race, 24 h HRV is still depressed: a wearable HRV that has not returned to baseline should be treated as supporting a longer hold, never as grounds to release early.
Because HRV tracks autonomic state and not tendomuscular damage, HRV and resting HR should not be used to shorten a 100-mile schedule; at most they may extend it or delay progression.
The engine should not expect HRV to normalise inside the first 7 days after a 100-mile race, so an HRV-based gate on a week-1 step would stay shut by design.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed esummary show a different author list from the record (Paech, Schrieber, Daehnert, Schmidt-Hellinger, Wolfarth, Wuestenfeld, Thouet); corrected. Abstract re-read (PMID 34046186); percentages, 1-week statement and conclusion match.
